conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Dr./Ms./Mr.] [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question tool that helps us see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, especially during the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting; it simply gives us a snapshot of your emotional health so we can support you in the best way possible.

Everything you share is confidential, and you can answer however feels right for you. We’ll go question by question, and if anything feels hard to talk about, we can pause. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

[small, tired smile] Honestly... it's been hard. I used to laugh at little things all the time—my husband's dumb jokes, silly videos—but lately it feels like I'm too worn out to even smile properly. Maybe once or twice this week I sort of chuckled, but it felt forced, like work. Mostly I just feel flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I smiled a little when the baby yawned, but it felt more like relief than actual laughter. Nothing really seems funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet pause, eyes on the floor]  
Not much… I keep telling myself I *should* feel excited about little outings—like when my mom offered to watch the baby so I could grab a coffee—but when the time comes I just feel… blah. Even the thought of putting on real clothes feels exhausting. I used to love Target runs, and now I can’t remember the last thing I actually *looked forward to*.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes... like last night when she wouldn't settle for two hours, I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I'm not feeding her right, or I'm missing some cue. My partner says she's just a baby and babies cry, but I still feel like it's my fault when I can't fix it immediately. It's not constant, but the thought pops up more than it should.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… a lot of the time. Even when she’s sleeping I catch myself staring at the monitor, convinced something’s wrong—like her breathing looks off or the room’s too warm. My heart races over the tiniest things: a hiccup, a red patch on her cheek, the way she flinches in her sleep. I *know* it’s probably normal baby stuff, but I can’t shake the “what-ifs.” It’s exhausting, and it happens almost every day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve had that sudden rush—like my chest tightens and I can’t get a full breath. It hits out of nowhere, even when the baby’s fine and the house is quiet. Nothing’s actually happening, but my body acts like there’s danger. It passes after a minute or two, but it leaves me shaky and even more tired.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days. Between feedings, diapers, and trying to sleep when she sleeps, it feels like I’m always one step behind. Yesterday I stood in the kitchen staring at a pile of bottles and just started crying because it felt like I’d never catch up. I keep telling myself “this is just new-mom stuff,” but the to-do list keeps growing and my energy keeps shrinking.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like my head won’t shut off. I’ll lie down exhausted, but then I start replaying every little thing: did I burp her long enough, did I fasten the car-seat straps right, am I already failing her and it’s only been a few weeks? It takes me forever to drift off, and when I do wake up for her next feed I’m still tense. Some nights I’m awake an hour or more just listening to her breathe.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve definitely had moments—usually in the late afternoon when I’m running on fumes. I’ll just feel this heavy sadness settle in, like I’m doing everything I can and it’s still not enough. It’s not all day, but yeah, most days there’s at least a stretch where I feel pretty low.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Once or twice this week, but not every day. The worst was when she wouldn’t latch during a night feeding—after twenty minutes I just handed her to my partner and burst into tears. It wasn’t really about the latch; it was like all the tiredness and worry spilled over at once.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I’ve never felt like hurting myself. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I want to be here for my baby—I just wish I didn’t feel so worn down all the time.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant ~2–4 wks old  
Instrument: EPDS-style 10-item questionnaire (self-report)

Symptoms / Behaviors endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment, loss of interest in previously pleasurable activities  
- Daily low mood, “heavy sadness,” frequent tearfulness (2× this week)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Persistent, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety; somatic anxiety (tachycardia, chest tightness) with abrupt panic episodes 3–4× weekly  
- Sleep-onset insomnia driven by ruminating thoughts; remains “tense” during overnight awakenings  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, “one step behind,” daily crying spells

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days, worse late afternoon/evening, clearly beyond typical “baby blues” duration (>2 wks). No self-harm ideation.

Screening significance  
Total score estimate ≈ 12–13 (requires formal scoring). Meets threshold for possible major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder, rule-out peripartum major depressive episode.

Risk factors  
- Persistent sadness, anhedonia, guilt  
- Anxiety/panic interfering with daily function  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
- Acute feeling of inability to cope  
- Protective factor: strong infant attachment, denial of self-harm intent

Safety  
Denies suicidal or homicidal ideation; no self-harm thoughts reported. Continue to monitor.

Next steps  
1. Complete formal EPDS scoring and document total.  
2. Consider referral to reproductive psychiatry or perinatal MH specialty for diagnostic clarification and treatment planning.
